desc:
Given an array nums of positive integers and an integer m, look for a non-empty subset of the elements (chosen by index) whose sum is divisible by m.

Return the smallest possible size of such a subset, or -1 if there is none.

nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5], m = 5 -> 1    (the element 5)
nums = [3, 5, 6],       m = 7 -> 3    (3 + 5 + 6 = 14)
nums = [2, 4],          m = 8 -> -1   (sums are 2, 4 and 6)
hints: Only the remainder of the running sum modulo m matters. How many different remainders are there?
Let dp[r] be the fewest elements of a non-empty subset (among the elements seen so far) whose sum has remainder r. Update it element by element, always reading the table from before the element.
For element x: first copy the table, then new[x % m] = min(new[x % m], 1), and for every r with dp[r] finite, new[(r + x) % m] = min(new[(r + x) % m], dp[r] + 1). The answer is dp[0].
editorial: Two subsets with the same remainder are interchangeable for the future, so the knapsack can be taken modulo m: the "weight" of an element is x mod m and the "capacity" wraps around. Define dp[r] as the minimum size of a non-empty subset of the processed elements with sum ≡ r (mod m), infinity if none exists.

For each element x we create a new table: copy the old one (do not take x), try the subset {x} on its own, and extend every existing subset by x, which moves the remainder from r to (r + x) mod m and adds one to the size. The answer is dp[0]; it counts only non-empty subsets because the empty subset is never inserted. Time O(n · m), space O(m).
A side note: if n ≥ m a valid subset always exists (a pigeonhole argument on prefix sums), but the answer can still be larger than 1, so the DP is needed to find the smallest.
